data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' grounded in the logical asymmetry of falsification and the goal of verisimilitude, not probability; accepting this costs us the comfort of believing our chosen theory is likely true, forcing us to act on the best-uncorroborated guess while acknowledging it may still be false.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be logically defined without invoking inductive assumptions about the future resembling the past.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for action implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature (that what worked before will work again).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'critical preference' and 'inductive belief' collapses under the pressure of practical decision-making where outcomes matter.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification of belief' (which requires induction and is rejected) and 'rational choice of action' (which relies on the logical status of having survived severe tests). A theory that has survived severe tests has higher informational content and closer proximity to truth (verisimilitude) than a refuted one, making it the only rational candidate for action without asserting its future success is probable.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
